description: Agent-based simulator of retail bank payments, calibrated against a sample of aggregated, anonymized real transactional data from a bank in Spain. Kaggle-hosted derivative commonly called "banksim1".
source: Lopez-Rojas, E.A., Axelsson, S. "BankSim: A Bank Payment Simulation for Fraud Detection Research." 26th European Modeling and Simulation Symposium (EMSS), Bordeaux, France, 2014.
https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ealaxi/banksim1 (dataset card: "Synthetic data from a financial payment system")
applicability_notes: `category` (es_transportation, es_food, es_health, es_travel, ... 15 values with an `es_` prefix denoting the original Spanish-market simulation) is a genuine merchant-category-code analog -- this is the strongest MCC comparison point of the four reference datasets.
`step` is a simulated day index (0-179 over 180 days), not an hour -- BankSim has NO within-day time granularity, so it cannot support an hour-of-day comparison, only a day-level cadence check.

`customer` and `merchant` are anonymized IDs, so transaction-per-party and merchant-cardinality comparisons are structurally possible, but this file does not assert precise customer/merchant population counts: multiple secondary write-ups repeat a customer count in the low thousands and a merchant count in the low tens, but this pass could not independently re-confirm exact figures against a primary source, so no numeric value is asserted here -- treat BankSim's population scale as qualitatively small and fixed, not a cited number.

n_transactions.source: Kaggle dataset card (ealaxi/banksim1) and widely repeated in derivative write-ups.

n_days_simulated.source: Kaggle dataset card and BankSim paper (six-month simulated window).

fraud_count.source: Kaggle dataset card / widely repeated in EDA write-ups: 587,443 genuine + 7,200 fraudulent = 594,643.

fraud_rate.source: Derived from the two published counts above (7200 / 594643), not itself a directly quoted percentage.

category_distribution_approx.source: Rounded from figures commonly reported across multiple independent public EDA notebooks of the banksim1 dataset. Not from the original paper (which does not publish this exact per-category breakdown); treat as approximate. The reliable part is the shape: es_transportation dominates by an order of magnitude or more, es_food a distant second, and a long tail of low-frequency, higher-value categories (es_travel, es_leisure, es_hotelservices).

amount_by_category_shape.value: high-frequency categories (es_transportation, es_food) skew toward small amounts; low-frequency categories (es_travel, es_leisure) skew toward much larger amounts -- and fraud in the original data is disproportionately concentrated in those low-frequency, high-value categories
amount_by_category_shape.source: Consistent qualitative finding repeated across independent public EDA notebooks and downstream fraud-detection papers using banksim1; no single authoritative mean-by-category table is asserted here as a precise citation.

usable_for_validation_areas: amount_distribution_per_mcc (via category as the MCC analog -- the strongest of the four references for this area)
not_usable_for: transactions_per_party (no confidently sourced customer/merchant population count in this pass)
inter_arrival_time (day-granularity `step` cannot support sub-day inter-arrival comparison)
